baseline.primary_source: Jerry Devore, "Active Directory Hardening Series", Microsoft Core Infrastructure and Security Blog (series verified Aug 2026).
baseline.value_policy: Expected values are only carried where the source states them. A control whose exact value the source does not state is present with status 'needs_baseline_value', no expected values, and is excluded from scoring. Values are never inferred or guessed.
baseline.pending_value_source: Microsoft Security Baselines (Security Compliance Toolkit) and/or CIS Benchmarks — needed to close the 'needs_baseline_value' controls.

notes: Check types in this release: gpo-security-template (GptTmpl.inf [Registry Values]), gpo-registry-pol (Registry.pol and Preferences Registry.xml) and directory-state. A directory-state control names a fixed, read-only directory query in directory_check and asserts that it finds nothing: none is a pass, any is a fail listing them, and a query that fails is an error. The spec's other directory-state controls (DEVORE-02 SMBv1, which the directory cannot show; DEVORE-08 Protected Users; the rest of DEVORE-07) are not in the catalog yet.

registry_key is the full path including the value name (its last component). For gpo-registry-pol the evaluator splits the last component off to match Registry.pol's separate key/value fields; for gpo-security-template the whole path is one [Registry Values] key.

Rollout is phased, not binary: interim_expected is the audit/negotiate step and final_expected the enforced step, so a domain correctly mid-rollout reports rollout_state 'audit' and result 'pass', not a failure.

os_default records the value Windows uses when no GPO sets the key, and only where a Microsoft document states it. Such a finding is evaluated against the default and marked 'source: os-default', so an assumed value is never mistaken for an enforced one. It is deliberately absent where there is no default to cite — LdapEnforceChannelBinding, for one, has no such key by default (channel binding is off), which is precisely why configuring it matters. Two limitations are deliberate. A finding resting on a default is capped at rollout_state 'audit', because 'enforced' means Group Policy holds the value and nothing enforces a default. And os_default is a single value, so a default that depends on the machine's role cannot be expressed: DEVORE-06-SMB-SERVER-SIGNING-ALWAYS is 'Enabled' by Microsoft's table for domain controllers but 'Disabled' for member servers and clients. Making that expressible would need the evaluator to know which machines a GPO lands on, which a SYSVOL/GPO scan cannot see at all — so those controls carry no default and say why in missing_note, rather than asserting one role's default over the whole domain.

controls.title: Require NTLMv2 (LAN Manager authentication level)
controls.why_it_matters: NTLMv1 and LM responses can be cracked or relayed quickly, so anyone who captures one can sign in as that user.

microsoft_deadline.summary: Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 switch BlockNtlmv1SSO to enforce by default, blocking NTLMv1 credentials for signed-in users (unless Credential Guard is on).

controls.friendly_policy: Network security: LAN Manager authentication level
controls.interim_effect: Machines send only NTLMv2. This already changes behaviour: a device or server that only accepts LM or NTLMv1, such as an old NAS or copier, stops working with them. Domain controllers still accept anything until step 2.
controls.missing_note: No GPO sets the level. Windows Vista / Server 2008 and later behave as level 3 when it's unset, but nothing enforces that, and a value set in the past stays on the device (see TATTOOING below). So ADitor reports this as a failure rather than assuming it's fine.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 1 lists levels 0-5 and what each means (3 = Send NTLMv2 response only; 5 = Refuse LM & NTLM).
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level'. Set every client and member server to 'Send NTLMv2 response only' (3) first. Only then raise domain controllers to 'Refuse LM & NTLM' (5).
caveats: IN STAGES: don't set domain controllers to 5 until every device is at 3 or higher. At 5, a DC treats NTLMv1 attempts as bad passwords, which locks accounts out (Devore saw 46 failed logons from one NTLMv1 SMB connection).
Levels 0-3 control what a client sends; levels 4-5 control what a server or DC accepts.
TATTOOING: the value lives outside HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies, so if you later set the policy back to 'Not Defined', the old value stays on each device and has to be cleared there.
Credential Guard disables NTLMv1 by itself and ignores this setting. No reboot is required.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Look for event 4624 with LmPackageName = 'NTLM V1' on member servers and endpoints, ignoring ANONYMOUS LOGON. Event 4776 on DCs doesn't record the NTLM version, so it can't be used for this.

controls.title: Domain controller LDAP server signing
controls.why_it_matters: Unsigned LDAP binds can be intercepted and relayed to a domain controller, letting an attacker act as the user who signed in.
controls.interim_effect: Signing is negotiated, not required. This is the Windows default, so on its own it changes nothing; the audit comes from LDAP diagnostic logging and event 2889 (DEVORE-03-LDAP-DIAG-LOGGING).
controls.missing_note: No GPO sets the LDAP signing requirement, so the DC still accepts unsigned simple binds over unencrypted LDAP.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 3 gives the values: 1 = None (signing is negotiated, not required) and 2 = Require signing.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Domain controller: LDAP signing requirements' = 'Require signing', in a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU. Before you do, check that event 2889 shows no unsigned binds.
caveats: AUDIT FIRST: don't require signing until event 2889 shows no unsigned binds.
A load balancer that terminates or bridges TLS forwards unsigned traffic, and shows up in event 2889 as the client IP.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Set '16 LDAP Interface Events' to 2, then watch event 2889 (each unsigned bind, with the client IP and account). Event 2887 gives the daily number of unsigned binds.

controls.title: LDAP client signing requirement
controls.why_it_matters: Makes Windows clients sign their LDAP traffic, so it can't be altered or relayed in transit.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: LDAP client signing requirements
controls.interim_effect: Clients ask for signing wherever the server supports it. This is the Windows default, so nothing breaks.
controls.os_default_source: Microsoft, 'Network security: LDAP client signing requirements', Default values table: the default is 'Negotiate signing' for domain controllers, member servers and client computers: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-ldap-client-signing-requirements. It's cited separately from the value mapping because the two come from different statements, and this one is what allows an unset value to be judged as 1.
controls.missing_note: No GPO sets this, so clients use the Windows default, Negotiate signing (1). They do ask for signing, but nothing in Group Policy keeps it that way, and a GPO could lower it to 0.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 3 gives the values 0/1/2 (None / Negotiate signing / Require signing). Microsoft documents the default as 'Negotiate signing' for domain controllers, member servers and client computers, in the Default values table of 'Network security: LDAP client signing requirements': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-ldap-client-signing-requirements
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LDAP client signing requirements' = 'Require signing'. Windows already negotiates signing without a GPO, so setting 'Negotiate signing' explicitly only documents the default; it doesn't harden anything.
caveats: Because Windows defaults to Negotiate (1), Windows SASL binds keep working when DCs start requiring signing, unless a GPO has lowered this to 0.

OS DEFAULT, NOT ENFORCED: where no GPO sets this, the result rests on the documented Windows default and is marked 'source: os-default'. That's a pass at the Negotiate step, not proof that nothing will set it to 0 later.

controls.title: Turn on LDAP Interface diagnostic logging (to find unsigned binds)
controls.why_it_matters: Records which clients still make unsigned LDAP binds, so you know what would break before you require signing.
controls.missing_note: No GPO sets the diagnostic level. Devore sets it with a registry write on each domain controller, which leaves nothing in Group Policy, so its absence here doesn't mean the level is 0 or that 2889 events aren't being logged. This scan reads Group Policy only and can't tell either way.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 3 gives 2. ADitor accepts 2 or higher, not exactly 2: Microsoft documents the NTDS diagnostic levels as 0-5, more verbose as they rise (default 0), in 'How to configure Active Directory and LDS diagnostic event logging': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/active-directory/configure-ad-and-lds-event-logging. A DC at 3 logs everything a DC at 2 does, including the 2889 events this check is for, so it isn't a failure.
controls.remediation: On domain controllers, set the '16 LDAP Interface Events' diagnostic level to 2 or higher while you collect unsigned-bind evidence. Devore does this with a registry write on each DC: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Diagnostics" /v "16 LDAP Interface Events" /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f. A GPO registry preference with the same value works the same way, and it's the only form this scan can see.
caveats: NOT SET THROUGH GROUP POLICY: the documented fix writes the registry directly on each domain controller, so this scan can't confirm the level. Where no GPO sets it, the result is 'unknown', not 'fail', and the finding includes the reg query command to check it on the DCs.
This turns on logging; it doesn't harden anything by itself. It produces events 2889 (client IP, account, bind type), 2887 (daily unsigned count) and 2888 (binds rejected once signing is required).
Left on permanently it's noisy, so it's usually raised only for the audit period.

Levels run 0-5, more verbose as they rise (Microsoft, 'AD and LDS diagnostic event logging'; default 0). A level above 2 logs more, including the 2889 events, so it passes. The minimum is 2; it doesn't have to be exactly 2.

controls.title: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos (disable RC4 on devices)
controls.why_it_matters: Kerberos tickets encrypted with RC4 can be cracked offline much faster than AES ones.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos
controls.baseline_gap: Devore Part 4 names only the policy and the msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute; it gives neither the registry path nor the bitmask. Both need to come from the Microsoft Security Baseline (Security Compliance Toolkit) or the CIS Benchmark before this can be checked.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos'. Enable the AES types. Clear RC4 only after 4768 auditing shows every device advertises AES. Fix service accounts before devices.
caveats: The source doesn't give the registry path, so this isn't checked yet.
Fix service accounts before disabling RC4 on devices.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Event 4768, Ticket Encryption Type. From the January 2025 cumulative update, 4768 and 4769 also show Advertised Etypes and Available Keys.

controls.title: Disable RC4 at the domain level on domain controllers
controls.why_it_matters: While domain controllers still issue RC4 tickets, any account with an SPN is easier to crack offline (Kerberoasting).

microsoft_deadline.summary: Domain controllers with the Kerberos updates treat accounts with no encryption-type setting as AES only (0x18). From July 2026 the rollback setting is gone.

controls.missing_note: No GPO sets the KDC default. Devore creates this value directly on the domain controllers, which leaves nothing in Group Policy, so its absence here doesn't mean RC4 is still allowed domain-wide. This scan reads Group Policy only and can't tell either way.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 4 gives 0x38 (56 decimal), citing KB5021131. ADitor accepts any AES-only value, not just 0x38: an AES bit (0x8 or 0x10) set and no DES or RC4 bit (0x1, 0x2, 0x4). So 0x18 (AES128 and AES256 without the AES session-key bit) passes too, while anything that includes RC4, such as 0x3C, fails.
controls.remediation: On domain controllers, set DefaultDomainSupportedEncTypes to 0x38. Do it last, after each service account has AES. Devore creates the value directly on the DCs; a GPO registry preference with the same value works the same way, and it's the only form this scan can see.
caveats: Devore warns that switching everything at once is 'too aggressive for most'. Make this the last step, after fixing individual accounts, not the first.

NOT SET THROUGH GROUP POLICY: the documented fix creates the value on the domain controllers, so its absence from Group Policy proves nothing. Where no GPO sets it, the result is 'unknown', not 'fail', and the finding includes the reg query command to check it on the DCs. Where a GPO does set it, for example as a registry preference, it's checked normally.
controls.audit_before_enforce: 4768 Ticket Encryption Type = RC4 identifies the accounts and devices that still depend on RC4.

controls.title: Service accounts with an SPN state AES in msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
controls.why_it_matters: A service account without AES gets RC4 tickets, the easiest kind to crack offline (Kerberoasting).

microsoft_deadline.summary: Domain controllers with the Kerberos updates treat accounts with no encryption-type setting as AES only (0x18). From July 2026 the rollback setting is gone.

controls.value_source: Devore Part 4: service accounts with an SPN should carry the AES bits in msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes. AES bits per Microsoft: 0x8 (AES128) and 0x10 (AES256). A blank value makes the account use the domain default, which depends on patch level: before the 2026 Kerberos updates the domain controllers assume 0x27 (RC4 tickets); from April 2026 (enforcement enabled) and July 2026 (automatic) they assume AES only (0x18), per Microsoft's CVE-2026-20833 guidance: https://support.microsoft.com/en-gb/topic/how-to-manage-kerberos-kdc-usage-of-rc4-for-service-account-ticket-issuance-changes-related-to-cve-2026-20833-1ebcda33-720a-4da8-93c1-b0496e1910dc. An account that explicitly lists RC4 without AES keeps getting RC4 tickets after those updates.
controls.remediation: For each listed service account, add the AES bits to msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes (0x8 for AES128, 0x10 for AES256). Setting it explicitly makes the account's behaviour the same whatever the domain controllers' patch level. Do this before disabling RC4 at the domain level, which is the last step of the Part 4 rollout.
caveats: An account whose password was set before the domain supported AES may have no AES keys yet; resetting its password generates them. Accounts migrated with ADMT are the usual case. On domain controllers with the 2026 Kerberos updates enforced, a blank account without AES keys can fail to authenticate rather than fall back to RC4.
An account listed as 'RC4 and no AES' keeps using RC4 even after the 2026 updates, because its explicit setting overrides the new AES-only default.

User accounts and managed service accounts (sMSA, gMSA) with an SPN are checked. Computer accounts are skipped: Windows computers maintain this attribute themselves. Non-Windows devices with an SPN (a NAS, a Linux host) don't, and are not checked here.
Disabled accounts and krbtgt are not listed.

A pass means nothing the bind account can read matched. AD silently leaves out objects and attributes an account isn't allowed to read, so run the scan with an account that can read the whole domain (an ordinary domain user can by default); a domain whose permissions were tightened can hide findings from a weaker account.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Event 4769 (and 4768) with Ticket Encryption Type 0x17 (RC4) shows which accounts and services still get RC4 tickets.

controls.title: Domain controller LDAP channel binding
controls.why_it_matters: Channel binding stops an attacker relaying someone's LDAPS sign-in to a domain controller.
controls.friendly_policy: Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements
controls.interim_effect: Domain controllers check the channel binding token from every client that sends one, and still accept clients that send none. That already rejects clients whose token doesn't match, which is common behind load balancers that terminate TLS, so test first.
controls.missing_note: The value isn't set, so channel binding is off (it has no default) and SASL binds over TLS aren't tied to the TLS channel.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 5 gives the registry path and the setting names, but not the numbers. The mapping 0/1/2 = Never / When supported / Always is Microsoft's, from KB4034879.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements' = 'When supported' (1) while you audit, then 'Always' (2).
caveats: Devore gives the setting names (Never / When supported / Always) but not the numbers. The 0/1/2 mapping is the widely used one from KB4034879; confirm it against a baseline source.
Unset means off. It only affects SASL binds over TLS. Load balancers that terminate or bridge TLS break channel binding, and a load-balanced name (VIP FQDN) must be in the DC certificate's SAN.
AUDIT FIRST: Server 2019 and later log event 3075; Server 2016 and earlier only log 3039, when a bind is rejected. Both need '16 LDAP Interface Events' at 2 or higher.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Event 3075 (2019+) or 3039 (2016 and earlier) in the Directory Service log.

controls.title: SMB client always requires signing
controls.why_it_matters: Without SMB signing, an attacker can relay a captured sign-in to a file server and act as that user.
controls.friendly_policy: Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)
controls.missing_note: No GPO requires SMB signing on the client side, so outbound SMB is signed only when the server requires it. ADitor doesn't assume a Windows default here: the policy's documented default is Disabled, but Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require signing by default, so what an unset value means depends on the Windows version, which a GPO scan can't see.
controls.value_source: Microsoft, 'Overview of Server Message Block signing in Windows', for 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)': registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManWorkstation\Parameters, value RequireSecuritySignature, REG_DWORD, 0 (disable) or 1 (enable): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/smb-signing-overview. That 'always' means signing is required is from Microsoft, 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/microsoft-network-client-digitally-sign-communications-always. The key is written as Microsoft writes it ('LanMan', capital M). Real GPOs spell the service name several ways, and ADitor matches it regardless of case.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled, on endpoints and member servers as well as domain controllers.
caveats: NOT THE LEGACY SETTING: this isn't 'Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)' (EnableSecuritySignature). That's a different, weaker setting that only affects SMBv1: Microsoft says SMB2 and later ignore it, and recommends against it. A GPO setting EnableSecuritySignature = 1 doesn't satisfy this check, which doesn't read that value.
'(always)' applies to every SMB version and drops the session when the other side can't sign.

Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require SMB signing by default, so on those an unset value doesn't necessarily mean unsigned traffic. It's still not enforced by policy, which is what this check looks for.

controls.title: SMB server always requires signing
controls.why_it_matters: Without SMB signing, an attacker can relay a captured sign-in to this server and act as that user.
controls.friendly_policy: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)
controls.missing_note: No GPO requires SMB signing on the server side, so inbound SMB is signed only when the client requires it. ADitor doesn't assume a Windows default here: Microsoft's defaults table gives Enabled for domain controllers but Disabled for member servers and clients, so the default depends on the machine's role.
controls.value_source: Microsoft, 'Overview of Server Message Block signing in Windows', for 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)': registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters, value RequireSecuritySignature, REG_DWORD, 0 (disable) or 1 (enable): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/smb-signing-overview. That 'always' means signing is required is from Microsoft, 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/microsoft-network-server-digitally-sign-communications-always. The key is written as Microsoft writes it ('LanMan', capital M). Real GPOs spell the service name several ways, and ADitor matches it regardless of case.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled, on member servers and endpoints too, not only domain controllers.
caveats: NOT THE LEGACY SETTING: this isn't 'Digitally sign communications (if client agrees)' (EnableSecuritySignature). That's a different, weaker setting that only affects SMBv1: Microsoft says SMB2 and later ignore it, and recommends against it. A GPO setting EnableSecuritySignature = 1 doesn't satisfy this check, which doesn't read that value.
Devore is explicit that this belongs on endpoints and member servers too. Third-party appliances and multifunction printers are the usual devices that can't sign.
Domain controllers already require SMB signing for SYSVOL and NETLOGON; this check is about the policy that requires it everywhere else.

controls.title: Turn off LLMNR (multicast name resolution)
controls.why_it_matters: On the local network, an attacker can answer LLMNR name lookups (for example with Responder) and collect password hashes.
controls.missing_note: No policy turns LLMNR off, so an attacker on the local network can answer name lookups (for example with Responder) and put themselves in the middle.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > 'Turn off multicast name resolution' = Enabled (writes EnableMulticast = 0).
caveats: Devore gives the value explicitly. Turning LLMNR off removes one of the ways Responder-style adversary-in-the-middle attacks work.

controls.title: Disable NetBIOS-over-TCP name resolution (P-node)
controls.why_it_matters: NetBIOS broadcast name lookups can be answered by an attacker on the local network, who then collects password hashes.
controls.friendly_policy: MS Security Guide: NetBT NodeType configuration (SecGuide.admx)
controls.missing_note: NodeType isn't set to P-node, so NetBIOS name resolution by broadcast is still on and can be spoofed.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > MS Security Guide > 'NetBT NodeType configuration' = P-node (writes NodeType = 2). Requires SecGuide.admx from the Security Compliance Toolkit.
caveats: Devore gives the value explicitly. Setting it through a GPO needs SecGuide.admx from the Security Compliance Toolkit.

controls.title: Built-in privileged groups that should be empty have no members
controls.why_it_matters: Members of these groups can take over the domain, so any account sitting in them unused is a standing risk.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 7 lists these built-in groups as ones that should normally have no members. Each group is found by its well-known SID, not its name, so a localized or renamed group is still checked.
controls.remediation: Remove the members of each listed group. Where someone needs the rights a group carries, delegate the specific rights instead, or add them only for the duration of the task.
caveats: The built-in Administrator account is a member of Schema Admins and Group Policy Creator Owners by default, so expect this check to fail on a new domain. Remove it from both, and add it back only for as long as a schema or Group Policy change needs it.

Members are the group's direct members, any account whose memberOf names the group (a cross-check, since AD returns no member list for an empty group or one the bind account can't read), and any account that uses the group as its primary group (AD leaves those out of the member list). A nested group counts as one member and is not expanded.

Schema Admins and Incoming Forest Trust Builders exist only in the forest root domain: in a child domain they are noted and not checked, and in the forest root a missing one is an error. Storage Replica Administrators exists only with a newer schema and is noted if missing. Any other group that can't be found makes this control an error, never a pass.

A pass means nothing the bind account can read matched. AD silently leaves out objects and attributes an account isn't allowed to read, so run the scan with an account that can read the whole domain (an ordinary domain user can by default); a domain whose permissions were tightened can hide findings from a weaker account.

controls.title: No accounts other than domain controllers have unconstrained delegation
controls.why_it_matters: A computer with unconstrained delegation keeps the tickets of everyone who connects to it, admins included, so taking it over can mean taking over the domain.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 7: accounts trusted for delegation to any service (userAccountControl TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION, 0x80000) should be moved to constrained or resource-based constrained delegation. Writable domain controllers carry this flag by design and are excluded, recognised by their account type (a computer account with SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT, 0x2000), not by primary group.
controls.remediation: For each listed account, switch to constrained delegation or resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) for only the services it needs, then turn off 'Trust this computer/user for delegation to any service'.
caveats: Changing delegation can break the services that depend on it. Find out what each listed account delegates to before changing it, and change one at a time.
Only writable domain controllers are excluded. Read-only domain controllers don't carry this flag by design, so one that has it is listed, as is any user account, whatever its primary group.
Disabled accounts are listed and marked: re-enabling one brings the exposure back.

A pass means nothing the bind account can read matched. AD silently leaves out objects and attributes an account isn't allowed to read, so run the scan with an account that can read the whole domain (an ordinary domain user can by default); a domain whose permissions were tightened can hide findings from a weaker account.

controls.title: Audit incoming NTLM traffic
controls.why_it_matters: Shows which clients still use NTLM against this system, which you need to know before restricting it.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic
controls.missing_note: Incoming NTLM auditing isn't set up, so there's no record of which clients still use NTLM against this system. Microsoft says 'Not defined' is the same as Disable, which audits no NTLM traffic.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 8 gives the registry path. CITED: Microsoft, 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit incoming NTLM traffic' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-restrict-ntlm-audit-incoming-ntlm-traffic), lists the options (Disable / Enable auditing for domain accounts / Enable auditing for all accounts), says 'Not defined' is the same as Disable and audits nothing, and says the policy doesn't block any traffic. INFERRED, not printed by Microsoft: that Disable is stored as the numeric 0 and the other options as 1 or higher. WHY THE INFERENCE IS SAFE: an unset REG_DWORD reads as 0, and Microsoft says unset and Disable are the same. So the check is '1 or higher', and the exact level is shown as evidence, not judged. If the inference were wrong, the level would be mislabelled, but Disable still couldn't pass.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic' = 'Enable auditing for domain accounts' (or 'for all accounts').
caveats: MINIMUM, NOT EXACT LEVEL: 1 or higher means some auditing is on, and 0 fails as auditing turned off. Microsoft lists the options but not their numbers, so whether it audits domain accounts or all accounts is shown in the evidence, not judged. Read the value found if you need to know.

INFERRED, NOT CITED: Microsoft doesn't publish that 'Disable' is stored as 0 and the other options as 1 or higher. ADitor infers it from Microsoft's statement that the unset policy behaves as 'Disable'. 'Where the value comes from' explains why checking only a minimum is safe on that basis; the exact level is never judged.

WATCH OUT: some third-party write-ups mix up the Audit* and Restrict* values and say 2 here means 'deny all'. It doesn't. Microsoft says this audit policy doesn't block any traffic. Blocking is DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-INCOMING, which isn't checked yet because no source gives its value.
Rollout state 'enforced' here means the audit policy is fully set up, not that NTLM is blocked. Blocking is covered by the DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-* checks.
Logs events 8002 and 8003 in Microsoft/Windows/NTLM/Operational.

controls.title: Audit outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers
controls.why_it_matters: Shows which systems still send NTLM to other servers, which you need to know before restricting it.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers
controls.missing_note: Outgoing NTLM is neither audited nor restricted, so there's no record of outbound NTLM use, which you need before you can block it. Microsoft says 'Not defined' is the same as Allow all: the device allows all NTLM authentication requests.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 8 gives the registry path. CITED: Microsoft, 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-restrict-ntlm-outgoing-ntlm-traffic-to-remote-servers), lists the options (Allow all / Audit all / Deny all) and says 'Not defined' is the same as Allow all. INFERRED, not printed by Microsoft: that Allow all is stored as the numeric 0 and the other two as 1 or higher. WHY THE INFERENCE IS SAFE: an unset REG_DWORD reads as 0, and Microsoft says unset and Allow all are the same. So the check is '1 or higher', and the exact level is shown as evidence, not judged. If the inference were wrong, the level would be mislabelled, but Allow all still couldn't pass. A minimum can't tell Audit all from Deny all, so a pass here means 'at least audited', never 'blocked'. Blocking uses the same value and is DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-OUTGOING, which isn't checked yet because it needs the exact number for Deny all.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers' = 'Audit all' during the audit phase.
caveats: MINIMUM, NOT EXACT LEVEL: 1 or higher means outgoing NTLM is at least logged, and Allow all (0) fails. Which level is set (Audit all or Deny all) is shown in the evidence, not judged, because Microsoft doesn't publish the numbers.

INFERRED, NOT CITED: Microsoft doesn't publish that 'Allow all' is stored as 0 and the other options as 1 or higher. ADitor infers it from Microsoft's statement that the unset policy behaves as 'Allow all'. 'Where the value comes from' explains why checking only a minimum is safe on that basis; the exact level is never judged.

One value controls both auditing and blocking of outgoing NTLM; see DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-OUTGOING, which isn't checked yet because no source gives the number for Deny all. A pass here means at least audited. It doesn't mean outgoing NTLM is blocked.
Rollout state 'enforced' here means this audit check's target is met, not that outgoing NTLM is denied.

controls.title: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain (domain controllers)
controls.why_it_matters: Shows NTLM use across the domain from the domain controllers, which you need to know before restricting it.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain
controls.missing_note: In-domain NTLM auditing isn't set up on the domain controllers, so there's no record of NTLM use across the domain. Microsoft gives 'Not defined' as the default for every server type, and Disable logs no events.
controls.value_source: Devore Part 8 gives the registry path. CITED: Microsoft, 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-restrict-ntlm-audit-ntlm-authentication-in-this-domain), lists five options (Disable / Enable for domain accounts to domain servers / Enable for domain accounts / Enable for domain servers / Enable all), says Disable logs no events for incoming NTLM traffic, gives 'Not defined' as the default for every server type, and says the policy doesn't block traffic. INFERRED, not printed by Microsoft: that Disable is stored as the numeric 0 and the four Enable options as 1 or higher. WHY THE INFERENCE IS SAFE: an unset REG_DWORD reads as 0, and Microsoft treats unset and Disable as the same. So the check is '1 or higher', and the exact option is shown as evidence, not judged. If the inference were wrong, the option would be mislabelled, but Disable still couldn't pass. With five options the level matters more here than for the other audit checks: only 'Enable all' records everything.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain' = 'Enable all', in a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU.
caveats: MINIMUM, NOT EXACT LEVEL: 1 or higher means some in-domain auditing is on, and 0 fails as auditing turned off. The policy has five options (Disable and four Enable scopes) and Microsoft doesn't publish their numbers, so which one is set is shown in the evidence, not judged. 'Enable all' is the one that records everything.

INFERRED, NOT CITED: Microsoft doesn't publish that 'Disable' is stored as 0 and the four Enable options as 1 or higher. ADitor infers it from Microsoft's statement that the unset policy behaves as 'Disable'. 'Where the value comes from' explains why checking only a minimum is safe on that basis; the exact level is never judged.

WATCH OUT: this is an audit policy. Microsoft says it doesn't block any traffic; the deny options belong to DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-INDOMAIN, which isn't checked yet. No value here means NTLM is blocked.
Rollout state 'enforced' here means this audit policy's target is met, not that in-domain NTLM is blocked. Blocking is covered by DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-INDOMAIN.
Logs events 8004, 8005 and 8006.

controls.title: Block incoming NTLM traffic (final phase)
controls.why_it_matters: NTLM can be relayed and cracked. Blocking it removes those attacks, once nothing depends on it.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic
controls.baseline_gap: Devore Part 8 gives the three audit paths but no blocking path or value. MSV1_0\RestrictReceivingNTLMTraffic is the value name usually cited, but it isn't confirmed here and isn't used. The path and the number for 'Deny all domain accounts' need to come from the Microsoft Security Baseline or the CIS Benchmark.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic' = 'Deny all domain accounts'. Try it on Tier 0 systems and PAWs first.
caveats: The source gives no registry path or value, so this isn't checked yet.

Use 'Deny all domain accounts', not 'Deny all accounts', which breaks loopback and the System account. There are separate policies for server exceptions. Once blocking is on, events 4001-4006 replace 8001-8006.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Events 8002 and 8003 must be clean on the systems in scope before you block.

controls.title: Block outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers
controls.why_it_matters: NTLM can be relayed and cracked. Blocking it removes those attacks, once nothing depends on it.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers
controls.baseline_gap: The value name is known: MSV1_0\RestrictSendingNTLMTraffic, the same one the outgoing audit check (DEVORE-08-NTLM-AUDIT-OUTGOING) reads. But no Microsoft or CIS document consulted gives the number that means 'Deny all'. The audit check can still use this value because it only needs a floor (a minimum): the permissive option is 0 and every other option is 1 or higher, which follows from Microsoft's statement that unset means Allow all. Blocking needs the exact number for Deny all, which a minimum can't express ('1 or higher' also matches Audit all), and guessing it would report a domain that only audits as blocking. So the catalog leaves this check's registry key empty, and nothing can report it as checked. It becomes active once the number is sourced from a Microsoft Security Baseline or CIS Benchmark.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers' = 'Deny all', once the audit phase comes back clean.
caveats: Uses the same value as the outgoing audit check (DEVORE-08-NTLM-AUDIT-OUTGOING), which only checks for 1 or higher ('at least audited'). A pass there doesn't mean outgoing NTLM is blocked. This one isn't checked yet: it needs the Deny all number from a real source.
WATCH OUT: some third-party write-ups mix up the Audit* and Restrict* values and confidently give a number for 'Deny all'. This check waits for a real source so that it doesn't guess.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Events 8001 and 8002 (outbound NTLM) must be clean on the systems in scope.

controls.title: Block NTLM authentication in this domain (domain controllers, last step)
controls.why_it_matters: NTLM can be relayed and cracked. Blocking it domain-wide removes those attacks, once nothing depends on it.
controls.friendly_policy: Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain
controls.baseline_gap: Devore Part 8 gives neither the blocking path nor the deny values. Netlogon\Parameters\RestrictNTLMInDomain is the value name usually cited, but it isn't confirmed here and isn't used. The deny options differ by scope, so both the path and the values need to come from a baseline source.
controls.remediation: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain' = the deny option that fits, on domain controllers, as the very last step of the project.
caveats: The source gives no path or values, so this isn't checked yet.
The deny options differ by scope. Apply one at the very end, on DCs only.
controls.audit_before_enforce: Events 8004, 8005 and 8006 must be clean across the domain before you block.

controls.title: Print Spooler: no NTLM fallback on named pipes
controls.why_it_matters: Stops the print spooler's named-pipe listener falling back to weaker NTLM authentication.
controls.friendly_policy: Printers\Configure RPC connection/listener settings (prefer RPC over TCP)
controls.missing_note: This value only matters where RPC over named pipes has to stay. The preferred setup is RPC over TCP, where it's correctly left unset, so its absence is reported as not applicable, not as a failure.
controls.remediation: Prefer RPC over TCP. Where named pipes have to stay, set 'Configure RPC connection settings' / RpcNamedPipeAuthentication = 2 so the named-pipe listener doesn't fall back to unauthenticated NTLM.
caveats: Devore gives the value explicitly. Other NTLM fallback sources (RPC EPM, TryIPSPN, Kerberos LogLevel, MS-CHAPv2, DFS referrals) are named in the post without values.
